t.4.32.1: Then Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy heroes, having been duly instructed, entered the formidable cave-city of Kiṣkindhā at Rāma's command.
t.4.32.2: The monkeys stationed at the gate there, huge of body and of great strength, all stood with palms joined in reverence upon seeing Lakṣmaṇa.
t.4.32.3: Seeing that son of Daśaratha enraged and sighing heavily, the monkeys became frightened and did not gather around him.
t.4.32.4: That glorious one beheld the vast cave, made of jewels, divine, with groves in full bloom, delightful and strewn all over with gems.
t.4.32.6: It was adorned by monkeys who were sons of the gods and Gandharvas, able to assume any form at will, wearing celestial garlands and garments, and pleasing to behold.
t.4.32.5: The city was crowded with mansions and palaces, adorned with wares of many kinds, and graced with blossoming trees bearing fruits that fulfil every desire.
t.4.32.7: He beheld the city whose great highways were perfumed by the fragrances of sandal, aloe-wood and lotuses, and by the sweet-smelling scents of maireya liquors and honey-wines.
t.4.32.8: There Rāghava saw mansions of many storeys, like the tablelands of the Vindhya and Meru mountains, and he saw clear mountain streams.
t.4.32.9: He beheld the lovely dwelling of Aṅgada, and those of Mainda and Dvivida, of Gavaya and Gavākṣa, and of Gaja and Śarabha.
t.4.32.10: Of Vidyunmālin and of Sampāti, of Sūryākṣa and of Hanumān, of Vīrabāhu and of Subāhu, and of the great-souled Nala.
t.4.32.12: Along the royal road Lakṣmaṇa saw the splendid, richly furnished mansions of these great-souled chiefs of the monkeys.
t.4.32.11: Of Kumuda and of Suṣeṇa, and likewise of Tāra and Jāmbavān, of Dadhivaktra, of Nīla, and of Supāṭala and Sunetra.
t.4.32.13: He saw mansions gleaming like pale white clouds and hung with heavenly garlands, rich in abundant wealth and grain, and made beautiful by jewels among women.
t.4.32.14: The delightful palace of the lord of the monkeys, hard to approach, was encircled by a pale white mountain and resembled the abode of the great Indra.
t.4.32.15: It was adorned with costly palace pinnacles resembling the peaks of Kailāsa, and with flowering trees that yielded fruits granting every desire.
t.4.32.16: It is graced with splendid trees bestowed by Mahendra, resembling dark rain-clouds, bearing divine flowers and fruits, casting cool shade, and delightful to the mind.
t.4.32.18: The mighty Saumitri, unhindered, entered the delightful abode of Sugrīva, as the sun enters a great cloud.
t.4.32.17: Its gate was surrounded by mighty monkeys with weapons in hand; it was bright, covered with heavenly garlands, and had archways of refined gold.
t.4.32.19: That righteous-souled one, having passed through the seven courtyards crowded with carriages and seats, beheld the vast inner apartments, very large and well guarded.
t.4.32.20: It was adorned here and there with couches of gold and silver and with many excellent seats spread with costly coverings.
t.4.32.22: And in Sugrīva's palace that mighty one saw many women of varied forms, proud of their beauty and youth.
t.4.32.21: Even as he was entering, he heard a continuous, sweet-toned sound, filled with the music of strings and song, its words and syllables sung in even harmony.
t.4.32.23: Having seen women of noble birth, wearing wreaths woven of many-colored flowers, busily occupied in making fine garlands, and adorned with the most excellent ornaments,
t.4.32.24: Lakṣmaṇa observed that Sugrīva's attendants, too, were none of them discontented, none overly agitated, and none lacking in splendid attire and accoutrements.
t.4.32.25: Then he saw Sugrīva, radiant like the sun, seated upon a supreme golden throne furnished with a costly covering.
t.4.32.27: The hero, seated on a splendid throne, his complexion like the finest gold, holding Rumā in a tight embrace, large-eyed himself, beheld Saumitri, whose spirit was undaunted and whose eyes were very large.
t.4.32.26: Him, glorious and of divine form, his limbs brilliant with celestial ornaments, wearing divine garlands and garments, invincible like the great Indra, surrounded by young women adorned with celestial ornaments and garlands.
